The plant has alternate, mostly sessile (at least on the upper parts of the branches), and stipulate leaves that are sticky, pubescent and have a kind of stinky smell. The flowers are small and tubular, with white corollas of 5 connate petals that have outward pointing lobes, and 5 connate sepals. The fruits are capsules with tiny seeds (seen as tiny black dots stuck to the sticky herbage in the pressed specimen).

Indian Tobacco (Nicotiana quadrivalvis) Native, annual, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 3-20 dm (up to 6.5 ft) tall on open, dry slopes and in well-drained washes. It is a fire-follower. Flowers are white and “salverform” (a slender tube that flares abruptly into a nearly flat portion at the open end). Flowers are fully open for only a few hours in the morning. The plant is leafy. Cauline leaves are generally lanceolate, not clasping, and sessile (NO petiole), except near base of plant. Upper leaves are reduced in size. N. quadrivalvis is similar to Many-flowered Tobacco (N. acuminata var. multiflora), but can be distinguished by the more sessile leaves. Flowers of N. quadrivalvis are also slightly larger, with the tube being 25–50 mm long, and the 5 petals 20–50 mm across. Peak bloom time: May-October.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. 42 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+quadrivalvis

Indian Tobacco (Nicotiana quadrivalvis) Native, annual, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 3-20 dm (up to 6.5 ft) tall on open, dry slopes and in well-drained washes. It is a fire-follower. Flowers are white and “salverform” (a slender tube that flares abruptly into a nearly flat portion at the open end). Flowers are fully open for only a few hours in the morning. The plant is leafy. Cauline leaves are generally lanceolate, not clasping, and sessile (NO petiole), except near base of plant. Upper leaves are reduced in size. N. quadrivalvis is similar to Many-flowered Tobacco (N. acuminata var. multiflora), but can be distinguished by the more sessile leaves. Flowers of N. quadrivalvis are also slightly larger, with the tube being 25–50 mm long, and the 5 petals 20–50 mm across. Peak bloom time: May-October.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. 42 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+quadrivalvis

description:
It’s bright yellow flowers caught our eye from a distance. 

Tree Tobacco (Nicotiana glauca) is an introduced/naturalized, large shrub or small tree in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 2-8m (up to 26ft) tall in open flats or slopes, and in disturbed soil. Tree tobacco is native to South America but it is now widespread as an introduced species on other continents. Leaves are relatively large, glabrous, glaucous, blue-green, broadly ovate, and 5-21 cm long. Inflorescence is many clusters of narrow, yellow, tubular, 3 -3.5 cm long flowers that are slightly flared at terminal end. Peak bloom time: April-August.
Indigenous people of North America and Hawaii had many medicinal uses for this plant, besides being smoked for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. 42 traditional uses are described here:

Native American Ethnobotany: (42 uses of Tree Tobacco) http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+glauca

Indian Tobacco (Nicotiana quadrivalvis) Native, annual, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 3-20 dm (up to 6.5 ft) tall on open, dry slopes and in well-drained washes. It is a fire-follower. Flowers are white and “salverform” (a slender tube that flares abruptly into a nearly flat portion at the open end). Flowers are fully open for only a few hours in the morning. The plant is leafy. Cauline leaves are generally lanceolate, not clasping, and sessile (NO petiole), except near base of plant. Upper leaves are reduced in size. N. quadrivalvis is similar to Many-flowered Tobacco (N. acuminata var. multiflora), but can be distinguished by the more sessile leaves. Flowers of N. quadrivalvis are also slightly larger, with the tube being 25–50 mm long, and the 5 petals 20–50 mm across. Peak bloom time: May-October.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. 42 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+quadrivalvis

The upper leaves are reduced in size, densely glandular-hairy, with a strong, unpleasant smell. This species is identified by the dark green stripes on its narrowly lanceolate calyx lobes. The petioled leaves and the dark stripe on the calyx lobes distinguish this from Indian Tobacco. Also, the flowers are smaller, the tube 30–40 mm long and 10–20 mm across. The plant is not uncommon in the south eastern parts of the county within the Diablo range, but has only recently been found elsewhere."

Indian Tobacco (Nicotiana quadrivalvis) Native, annual, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 3-20 dm (up to 6.5 ft) tall on open, dry slopes and in well-drained washes. It is a fire-follower. Flowers are white and “salverform” (a slender tube that flares abruptly into a nearly flat portion at the open end). Flowers are fully open for only a few hours in the morning. The plant is leafy. Cauline leaves are generally lanceolate, not clasping, and sessile (NO petiole), except near base of plant. Upper leaves are reduced in size. N. quadrivalvis is similar to Many-flowered Tobacco (N. acuminata var. multiflora), but can be distinguished by the more sessile leaves. Flowers of N. quadrivalvis are also slightly larger, with the tube being 25–50 mm long, and the 5 petals 20–50 mm across. Peak bloom time: May-October.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. 42 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+quadrivalvis

Desert Tobacco (Nicotiana obtusifolia) Native, perennial, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 1 - 2.5 ft tall on rocky slopes or in gravelly desert washes. Large leaves clasp at the base. Corolla and throat is a one inch long tubular, green-white or dull white flower. Peak bloom time: March-June.
Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked by Indigenous people for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. Coachella Valley Preserve: For thousands of years, particles of sand from the San Bernardino Mountains and Indio Hills washed into the Coachella Valley forming a system of sand dunes. Today, these dunes are part of the Coachella Valley Preserve System, a 20,000-acre sanctuary.
The Coachella Valley Preserve also contains several palm oases that sit on top of San Andreas Fault lines. Underground water rises to the surface through these cracks. California Fan Palms (Washingtonia filifera) grow along the cracks where the water seeps up creating a desert oases. Many plant species thrive in the alkaline soil.
Coachella Valley sits at the convergence of four vast ecological systems - the Colorado (or Sonoran) Desert, the Mojave Desert, and the coastal and peninsular mountain ranges.

Indian Tobacco (Nicotiana quadrivalvis) Native, annual, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 3-20 dm (up to 6.5 ft) tall on open, dry slopes and in well-drained washes. It is a fire-follower. Flowers are white and “salverform” (a slender tube that flares abruptly into a nearly flat portion at the open end). Flowers are fully open for only a few hours in the morning. The plant is leafy. Cauline leaves are generally lanceolate, not clasping, and sessile (NO petiole), except near base of plant. Upper leaves are reduced in size. N. quadrivalvis is similar to Many-flowered Tobacco (N. acuminata var. multiflora), but can be distinguished by the more sessile leaves. Flowers of N. quadrivalvis are also slightly larger, with the tube being 25–50 mm long, and the 5 petals 20–50 mm across. Peak bloom time: May-October.
Indigenous people had many uses for this plant. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. 42 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+quadrivalvis

Manyflower Tobacco (Nicotiana acuminata var. multiflora) Introduced/naturalized, annual, densely glandular-hairy plant in the Genus Tobacco (Nicotiana) and Nightshade (Solanaceae) family. It grows 50–150 cm (up to 6 ft) tall in open, sandy or gravelly areas. It is densely glandular-hairy. Cauline leaves are petioled. Flower: Calyx is dark-striped, lobes are narrowly lanceolate, unequal, generally ± >= tube, not pock-marked. Peak bloom time: April–October.

Jepson eFlora does not recognize species alone, only Nicotiana acuminata var. multiflora

"This is similar to Indian Tobacco (N. quadrivalvis). The plant itself is very leafy, the leaves being petioled and ovate. The upper leaves are reduced in size, densely glandular-hairy, with a strong, unpleasant smell. This species is identified by the dark green stripes on its narrowly lanceolate calyx lobes. The petioled leaves and the dark stripe on the calyx lobes distinguish this from Indian Tobacco. Also, the flowers are smaller, the tube 30–40 mm long and 10–20 mm across. The plant is not uncommon in the south eastern parts of the county within the Diablo range, but has only recently been found elsewhere."

description:
White-flowering Desert Tobacco growing in a semi-shaded desert wash in rocky Upper Carrizo Canyon. (I sure miss my Iphone 12 mini which took much sharper photos!)

Desert Tobacco (Nicotiana obtusifolia) is a native, perennial, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 1 - 2.5 ft tall on rocky slopes and in gravelly desert washes in Creosote Bush Scrub and Joshua Tree Woodland plant communities. Large leaves clasp at the base. Corolla is +- funnel-shaped, green-white or dull white, and tube plus throat is 15--26 mm long. Peak bloom time: March-June. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked by Indigenous people for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. Tobacco is the sacred plant of the Cahuilla, the indigenous people of the Coachella Valley. 22 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+obtusifolia

description:
Desert Tobacco (Nicotiana obtusifolia) is a native, perennial, glandular-hairy plant in the Nightshade (Solanaceae) family that grows 1 - 2.5 ft tall on rocky slopes and in gravelly desert washes in Creosote Bush Scrub and Joshua Tree Woodland plant communities. Large leaves clasp at the base. Corolla is +- funnel-shaped, green-white or dull white, and tube plus throat is 15--26 mm long. Peak bloom time: March-June. Parts of the plant were dried, processed, and smoked by Indigenous people for the alkaloid chemical nicotine effects. Tobacco is the sacred plant of the Cahuilla, the indigenous people of the Coachella Valley. 22 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Nicotiana+obtusifolia
